questionText: A 68-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea and two episodes of exertional syncope over the past 3 months. On examination, his blood pressure is 118/78 mmHg, heart rate is 74 bpm and regular, and there is a slow-rising carotid pulse with a harsh 3/6 mid-systolic murmur radiating to the carotids and a soft second heart sound. Transthoracic echocardiography reveals a heavily calcified trileaflet aortic valve with a mean pressure gradient of 48 mmHg, peak aortic jet velocity of 4.4 m/s, and calculated aortic valve area of 0.75 cm². Left ventricular ejection fraction is 58%. Coronary angiography shows no significant obstructive coronary artery disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive management?
optionA: Commence ramipril and review with repeat echocardiography in 6 months
optionB: Aortic valve replacement
optionC: Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as standalone therapy
optionD: Commence metoprolol and furosemide for symptom control
explanation: This patient has symptomatic severe high-gradient aortic stenosis (peak velocity >= 4.0 m/s, mean gradient >= 40 mmHg, valve area < 1.0 cm²). Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis carries a dismal prognosis without valve intervention (average survival 2-3 years after syncope or heart failure onset). Definitive aortic valve replacement (surgical AVR or transcatheter aortic valve implantation [TAVI] depending on surgical risk and Heart Team assessment) is a Class I indication. Medical therapy does not slow disease progression, and balloon valvuloplasty alone provides only transient haemodynamic relief with high restenosis rates.

questionText: A 34-year-old man is referred to the cardiology clinic following the sudden unexplained nocturnal death of his 31-year-old brother. He is asymptomatic and takes no regular medications. His resting 12-lead ECG demonstrates a coved-type ST-segment elevation of 3 mm in leads V1 and V2 followed by a negative T wave, with structurally normal cardiac chambers on transthoracic echocardiography. Which ion channel gene mutation is most commonly implicated in this inherited arrhythmia syndrome?
optionA: KCNQ1 (potassium channel alpha-subunit)
optionB: RYR2 (cardiac ryanodine receptor)
optionC: SCN5A (cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel alpha-subunit)
optionD: MYH7 (beta-myosin heavy chain)
explanation: The ECG demonstrates a spontaneous Type 1 Brugada pattern (>= 2 mm coved ST-segment elevation followed by a negative T wave in right precordial leads V1-V2), diagnostic of Brugada syndrome in the context of family history of sudden cardiac death. Loss-of-function mutations in SCN5A, encoding the alpha-subunit of the cardiac sodium channel (Nav1.5), are the most common genetic cause (found in 20-30% of probands). KCNQ1 mutations cause LQT1, RYR2 mutations cause catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT), and MYH7 mutations cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

questionText: A 62-year-old woman with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 28% secondary to non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy) attends routine outpatient review. She remains in NYHA Class II dyspnoea despite optimal tolerated doses of sacubitril/valsartan, bisoprolol, and spironolactone. Her HbA1c is 5.4% (36 mmol/mol), eGFR is 54 mL/min/1.73m², and blood pressure is 114/70 mmHg. Which additional medication is most strongly indicated to reduce her risk of cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalisation?
optionA: Dapagliflozin
optionB: Digoxin
optionC: Ivabradine
optionD: Amlodipine
explanation: Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors such as dapagliflozin (DAPA-HF trial) and empagliflozin (EMPEROR-Reduced trial) significantly reduce the composite endpoint of cardiovascular mortality and worsening heart failure hospitalisation in patients with HFrEF (LVEF <= 40%), completely independent of diabetes status. They represent one of the four foundational pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy (ARNI/ACEi, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor).

questionText: A 72-year-old man presents with newly diagnosed non-valvular paroxysmal atrial fibrillation detected on Holter monitoring after transient palpitations. He has a history of well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus, with no prior stroke, TIA, or vascular disease. His renal function is normal (creatinine 82 umol/L, eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73m²). According to Australian Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines (CHA2DS2-VA score), what is his score and recommended antithrombotic strategy?
optionA: Score 1; anticoagulation should be considered
optionB: Score 2; oral anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) is recommended
optionC: Score 3; dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel is recommended
optionD: Score 3; oral anticoagulation with apixaban or rivaroxaban is recommended
explanation: The Australian NHFA/CSANZ guidelines use the sexless CHA2DS2-VA score. This patient receives 1 point for age 65-74 years, 1 point for hypertension, and 1 point for diabetes mellitus, giving a CHA2DS2-VA score of 3. A CHA2DS2-VA score >= 2 is a strong (Class I) indication for oral anticoagulation, with a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC such as apixaban, rivaroxaban, or dabigatran) preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF.

questionText: A 29-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation presents with blood pressure readings persistently around 158/102 mmHg without proteinuria or features of pre-eclampsia. She has no history of asthma or heart block. Which of the following oral antihypertensive agents is considered first-line and safe for managing hypertension in pregnancy?
optionA: Perindopril
optionB: Labetalol
optionC: Irbesartan
optionD: Spironolactone
explanation: First-line oral antihypertensive agents safe in pregnancy include labetalol (alpha/beta-blocker), methyldopa, and long-acting nifedipine. ACE inhibitors (perindopril) and angiotensin receptor blockers (irbesartan) are strictly contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetotoxicity (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia, and intrauterine growth restriction). Spironolactone is avoided due to anti-androgenic effects on a male fetus.

questionText: A 28-year-old man with known ulcerative colitis is admitted with acute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC), passing 10 bloody stools per day with a pulse of 98 bpm and CRP of 65 mg/L. He is commenced on intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg QID and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Flexible sigmoidoscopy confirms severe deep ulceration and biopsy rules out CMV colitis. On day 3 of IV corticosteroids, he continues to pass 9 bloody stools daily with a CRP of 52 mg/L. Abdominal X-ray shows no toxic megacolon. What is the most appropriate next step in medical management?
optionA: Continue intravenous hydrocortisone alone until day 7 before reassessing
optionB: Commence rescue therapy with intravenous infliximab or ciclosporin alongside colorectal surgical consultation
optionC: Switch intravenous hydrocortisone to oral azathioprine monotherapy
optionD: Commence oral mesalazine 4.8 g daily and discharge with early outpatient follow-up
explanation: By the Oxford (Travis) criteria on Day 3 of IV corticosteroid therapy, a stool frequency > 8/day or 3-8/day with CRP > 45 mg/L predicts an 85% likelihood of requiring colectomy during that admission if steroids are continued alone. Prompt initiation of medical rescue therapy with either infliximab or ciclosporin (which have comparable short-term efficacy in the CONSTRUCT and CYSIF trials), coupled with joint medical-surgical review, is essential.

questionText: A 56-year-old man with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis presents with mild abdominal discomfort and fever (38.1°C). Diagnostic paracentesis reveals ascitic fluid total protein of 11 g/L, albumin gradient (SAAG) of 18 g/L, and an ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) leukocyte count of 420 cells/mm³ (0.42 x 10⁹/L). Serum creatinine is 118 umol/L and bilirubin is 78 umol/L. In addition to intravenous third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone), which adjunctive therapy has been shown to significantly reduce the incidence of hepatorenal syndrome and inpatient mortality?
optionA: Intravenous concentrated albumin (1.5 g/kg on day 1, then 1.0 g/kg on day 3)
optionB: High-dose intravenous furosemide (80 mg BD)
optionC: Large-volume therapeutic paracentesis of 8 litres immediately
optionD: Oral propranolol titrated to heart rate 55 bpm
explanation: An ascitic fluid PMN count >= 250 cells/mm³ confirms spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). In patients with SBP, intravenous 20% concentrated albumin (1.5 g/kg within 6 hours of diagnosis and 1.0 g/kg on day 3, per Sort et al. NEJM) significantly decreases the incidence of type 1 hepatorenal syndrome (from 30% to 10%) and lowers inpatient mortality (from 29% to 10%). Non-selective beta-blockers and diuretics should be withheld during acute SBP with renal dysfunction.

questionText: A 51-year-old woman presents with fatigue and generalized pruritus for 6 months. Liver biochemistry reveals alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 410 U/L (normal < 110), GGT 320 U/L, ALT 58 U/L, AST 52 U/L, and total bilirubin 16 umol/L. Liver ultrasound shows a normal biliary tree with no duct dilatation or gallstones. Which serological autoantibody is the hallmark diagnostic marker for this condition?
optionA: Anti-smooth muscle antibody (ASMA)
optionB: Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) directed against the PDC-E2 subunit
optionC: Anti-liver kidney microsomal type 1 antibody (Anti-LKM1)
optionD: IgG4 subclass elevation
explanation: This middle-aged woman has a chronic intrahepatic cholestatic liver profile (markedly elevated ALP and GGT with normal extrahepatic bile ducts on ultrasound) and pruritus, classic for Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC). Anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA), specifically targeting the E2 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC-E2 / M2 antigen), are present in 90-95% of patients with PBC and have >95% specificity. First-line therapy is ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) 13-15 mg/kg/day.

questionText: A 44-year-old man is found to have persistently elevated serum ferritin of 1,450 ug/L and transferrin saturation of 68%. HFE genetic testing reveals C282Y homozygosity. Liver elastography (FibroScan) demonstrates a liver stiffness of 6.1 kPa, and serum ALT is normal. What is the most appropriate initial therapeutic targets and treatment for this patient?
optionA: Oral deferasirox chelation aiming for transferrin saturation < 20%
optionB: Therapeutic venesection (phlebotomy) aiming for serum ferritin 50–100 ug/L
optionC: Observation only until cirrhosis develops on biopsy
optionD: Dietary iron restriction alone without venesection
explanation: In C282Y homozygous hereditary haemochromatosis with elevated iron indices (ferritin > 300 ug/L in men and transferrin saturation > 45%), weekly or fortnightly therapeutic venesection (removing ~450-500 mL blood, ~250 mg iron per unit) is first-line treatment to prevent hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis, arthropathy, and diabetes. The induction target is a serum ferritin of 50-100 ug/L.

questionText: A 61-year-old woman with compensated Child-Pugh A cirrhosis secondary to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (MASLD) undergoes her routine surveillance hepatobiliary ultrasound. What is the standard guideline-recommended surveillance interval and test for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in patients with cirrhosis?
optionA: 6-monthly liver ultrasound with or without serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
optionB: Annual multiphase CT abdomen with intravenous contrast
optionC: 2-yearly liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast
optionD: 3-monthly serum AFP measurement alone
explanation: International and Australian consensus guidelines (AASLD, EASL, GESA) recommend 6-monthly abdominal ultrasound, with or without serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), for HCC surveillance in all patients with cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A and B, or Child-Pugh C awaiting liver transplantation) as well as high-risk non-cirrhotic chronic hepatitis B carriers. Combining ultrasound with AFP increases sensitivity for early-stage HCC detection compared with ultrasound alone.

questionText: A 67-year-old man with severe COPD (baseline FEV1 34% predicted) presents to the Emergency Department with worsening dyspnoea and purulent sputum. After 1 hour of controlled oxygen therapy (titrated to SpO2 88-92%), nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone, and antibiotics, his arterial blood gas on FiO2 0.28 shows: pH 7.28, PaCO2 68 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 31 mmol/L. He is alert and cooperative, with a respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation without pneumothorax or consolidation. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
optionA: Increase FiO2 to 0.60 via Hudson mask to achieve SpO2 > 96%
optionB: Commence bilevel non-invasive ventilation (NIV / BiPAP)
optionC: Proceed immediately to endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation
optionD: Administer intravenous acetazolamide to correct the elevated bicarbonate
explanation: In acute exacerbations of COPD complicated by acute or acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH 7.25–7.35 and PaCO2 > 45 mmHg) persisting despite optimal medical therapy and controlled oxygen targeting SpO2 88-92%, bilevel non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is strongly indicated (Number Needed to Treat ~10 to prevent mortality and ~4 to prevent intubation).

questionText: A 71-year-old man who is a lifelong non-smoker presents with an 18-month history of progressive dry cough and exertional dyspnoea. Examination reveals fine Velcro-like bibasal end-inspiratory crackles and finger clubbing. Autoimmune serology (ANA, ENA, RF, anti-CCP) is negative, and there is no history of occupational dust, bird, or mould exposure. High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest demonstrates subpleural, basal-predominant reticular opacities with traction bronchiectasis and honeycombing, without ground-glass attenuation. Spirometry shows FVC 72% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.84, and DLCO 54% predicted. Which medication has been shown to reduce the annual rate of FVC decline in this condition?
optionA: Combination prednisolone, azathioprine, and N-acetylcysteine
optionB: Nintedanib (or pirfenidone)
optionC: Rituximab
optionD: Inhaled fluticasone/salmeterol
explanation: This patient has classic clinical and HRCT features (definite Usual Interstitial Pneumonia [UIP] pattern: basal/subpleural predominance, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis) of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF). Antifibrotic therapy with nintedanib (an intracellular tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting FGFR, PDGFR, VEGFR; INPULSIS trials) or pirfenidone (ASCEND/CAPACITY trials) reduces the rate of FVC decline by approximately 50%. Combination prednisolone + azathioprine + NAC (PANTHER-IPF trial) increased mortality and hospitalisations in IPF and is contraindicated.

questionText: A 58-year-old woman with a right-sided pleural effusion undergoes diagnostic thoracentesis. Paired pleural fluid and serum results are as follows: Pleural fluid protein 38 g/L (Serum total protein 68 g/L); Pleural fluid LDH 190 U/L (Serum LDH 260 U/L; laboratory upper limit of normal for serum LDH is 220 U/L). According to Light's criteria, how is this effusion classified?
optionA: Transudate because pleural fluid LDH is below the serum upper limit of normal
optionB: Exudate because the pleural fluid-to-serum protein ratio is > 0.5
optionC: Transudate because both protein and LDH ratios are below threshold
optionD: Chylothorax requiring triglyceride measurement for confirmation
explanation: Light's criteria classify a pleural effusion as an exudate if at least ONE of the following three criteria is met: (1) Pleural fluid protein / Serum protein ratio > 0.5; (2) Pleural fluid LDH / Serum LDH ratio > 0.6; (3) Pleural fluid LDH > 2/3 (0.67) of the laboratory upper limit of normal for serum LDH. Here, the protein ratio is 38 / 68 = 0.56 (> 0.5) and the LDH ratio is 190 / 260 = 0.73 (> 0.6), clearly classifying the effusion as an exudate.

questionText: A 36-year-old woman presents with bilateral ankle erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest radiograph, and mild arthralgias. She is afebrile, asymptomatic from a respiratory standpoint, has normal spirometry and DLCO, normal serum calcium, and normal slit-lamp ocular examination. Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) of a mediastinal lymph node shows non-caseating epithelioid granulomas with negative mycobacterial and fungal stains/cultures. What is the most appropriate management?
optionA: Commence oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for 6 months
optionB: Observation and symptomatic NSAIDs without systemic corticosteroids
optionC: Commence methotrexate 15 mg weekly as steroid-sparing therapy
optionD: Commence standard four-drug antituberculous therapy empirically
explanation: This patient has Löfgren syndrome, an acute presentation of Stage I pulmonary sarcoidosis characterised by erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and migratory polyarthralgia. Löfgren syndrome carries an excellent prognosis with spontaneous remission occurring in >80-85% of patients within 1-2 years. In the absence of vital organ involvement (cardiac, neurological, ocular, hypercalcaemia, or progressive pulmonary impairment), observation and NSAIDs for joint/skin discomfort are appropriate rather than systemic corticosteroids.

questionText: A 64-year-old man undergoes evaluation for a solitary 18 mm spiculated right upper lobe pulmonary nodule detected on CT chest. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history. Pre-operative lung function testing shows an FEV1 of 2.1 L (78% predicted) and DLCO of 74% predicted. What is the most appropriate next investigation to stage this lesion prior to potential curative resection?
optionA: 18F-FDG PET-CT scan
optionB: Repeat low-dose CT chest in 12 months
optionC: Sputum cytology on three consecutive mornings
optionD: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) lung scintigraphy
explanation: For a solid, spiculated pulmonary nodule > 8-10 mm in a high-risk patient, 18F-FDG PET-CT is the standard staging modality to characterise metabolic activity of the primary lesion and evaluate for occult hilar/mediastinal nodal or distant metastases prior to tissue biopsy and anatomical surgical resection.

questionText: A 42-year-old man presents with a 5-day history of progressive symmetrical ascending limb weakness and paraesthesia following a Campylobacter jejuni diarrhoeal illness 2 weeks ago. On examination, he has 3/5 power in his lower limbs, 4/5 power in his upper limbs, and generalized areflexia. Nerve conduction studies show multifocal demyelination with conduction block, and CSF shows protein 1.1 g/L with 2 leukocytes/uL. Which parameter is the most reliable bedside physiological measure to monitor for impending neuromuscular respiratory failure requiring ICU intubation?
optionA: Continuous pulse oximetry (SpO2) on supplemental oxygen
optionB: Serial forced vital capacity (FVC) measurements
optionC: Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) after salbutamol
optionD: Daily venous bicarbonate concentration
explanation: In Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy), neuromuscular respiratory failure occurs in up to 20-30% of patients. Serial bedside Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) (along with Negative Inspiratory Force / Maximal Inspiratory Pressure) is the gold-standard physiological marker. By the '20/30/40 rule', an FVC < 20 mL/kg (or a >30% drop in FVC), MIP worse than -30 cmH2O, or MEP < 40 cmH2O indicates impending respiratory failure and the need for elective ICU intubation. Pulse oximetry and hypercapnia are late signs.

questionText: A 76-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of new right-sided temporal headache, scalp tenderness when combing her hair, and jaw pain when chewing food. Yesterday she experienced a 10-minute episode of painless monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax) in her right eye. Her ESR is 88 mm/hr and CRP is 74 mg/L. What is the most critical immediate management step?
optionA: Withhold corticosteroids until a temporal artery biopsy is performed in 3 days
optionB: Administer high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (e.g., 500–1000 mg daily) immediately
optionC: Commence oral prednisolone 15 mg daily as used for polymyalgia rheumatica
optionD: Order an outpatient carotid Doppler ultrasound before starting therapy
explanation: This patient has Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA / temporal arteritis) complicated by transient visual ischaemia (amaurosis fugax), which is a medical emergency carrying a high risk of permanent, irreversible bilateral blindness from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Immediate high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (500–1000 mg IV daily for 3 days followed by high-dose oral prednisolone) must be commenced without waiting for temporal artery biopsy or vascular ultrasound. Biopsy remains diagnostic within 1-2 weeks of starting steroids.

questionText: A 63-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history presents with proximal lower limb weakness and dry mouth. On neurological examination, hip flexion is initially 4-/5 with depressed patellar reflexes, but after 10 seconds of sustained maximal isometric contraction of the quadriceps, power transiently improves to 5/5 and the patellar tendon reflex becomes brisker. Autoantibodies against which target are most strongly associated with this disorder?
optionA: Post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (AChR)
optionB: Pre-synaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC)
optionC: Muscle-specific tyrosine kinase (MuSK)
optionD: Aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channel
explanation: Proximal lower limb weakness, autonomic dysfunction (dry mouth), hyporeflexia, and post-exercise facilitation (improvement in strength and reflexes following brief maximal contraction) are classic clinical hallmarks of Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS). Over 85-90% of patients with LEMS harbour autoantibodies against pre-synaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC), impairing calcium-dependent acetylcholine vesicle release. Approximately 50-60% of cases are paraneoplastic, associated with small-cell lung carcinoma (SCLC).

questionText: A 49-year-old woman is admitted to the neurosurgical ICU following endovascular coiling of a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm that caused an acute subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). Which medication should be administered enterally for 21 days to improve neurological outcomes and reduce delayed cerebral ischaemia?
optionA: Nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours
optionB: Dexamethasone 8 mg every 6 hours
optionC: Intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion
optionD: Clopidogrel 75 mg daily
explanation: Enteral nimodipine (60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days), a lipophilic dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is the only proven pharmacological intervention (Class I, Level A evidence) shown to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia (vasospasm-related infarction) and poor neurological outcome after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.

questionText: A 31-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis is being considered for natalizumab (an anti-alpha-4 integrin monoclonal antibody). Prior to initiating natalizumab and every 6 months during therapy, serological testing for antibodies against which virus is mandatory to stratify the risk of Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML)?
optionA: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)
optionB: JC polyomavirus (JCV)
optionC: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV)
optionD: Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
explanation: Natalizumab blocks alpha-4 integrin (VLA-4)-mediated lymphocyte trafficking across the blood-brain barrier and carries a known risk of Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML), an opportunistic demyelinating brain infection caused by reactivation of latent John Cunningham (JC) polyomavirus. Risk stratification requires anti-JCV antibody status and index testing, assessment of prior immunosuppressant exposure, and treatment duration (>24 months).

questionText: A 38-year-old man with newly diagnosed advanced HIV infection (CD4 count 24 cells/uL, HIV viral load 420,000 copies/mL) presents with a 2-week history of worsening headache, fever, and photophobia. Lumbar puncture reveals an opening pressure of 34 cmH2O, CSF white cell count 18/uL (lymphocytic), protein 0.95 g/L, glucose 1.8 mmol/L, and a positive CSF cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) and India ink stain for Cryptococcus neoformans. He is commenced on induction antifungal therapy with liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine. When should antiretroviral therapy (ART) be initiated?
optionA: Immediately on the same day as antifungal induction therapy
optionB: Deferred for 4 to 6 weeks after starting antifungal therapy
optionC: Deferred until his CD4 count rises above 200 cells/uL spontaneously
optionD: Within 48 hours alongside high-dose intravenous dexamethasone
explanation: In HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, the COAT trial (Boulware et al., NEJM) demonstrated that early ART initiation (within 1-2 weeks of antifungal diagnosis) significantly increased 26-week mortality compared with deferred ART initiation (at 4-6 weeks), largely driven by fatal central nervous system Cryptococcal Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (CNS-IRIS) in a closed cranial vault. Routine adjunctive dexamethasone was also shown in the CryptoDex trial to increase disability and slow fungal clearance.

questionText: A 52-year-old man from Darwin with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and hazardous alcohol intake presents during the tropical wet season with high fevers, rigors, and septic shock. Chest X-ray shows cavitating right upper lobe pneumonia, and CT abdomen reveals multiple small splenic abscesses. Blood cultures grow a Gram-negative bacillus with bipolar 'safety-pin' staining that is intrinsically resistant to gentamicin and colistin. What is the causative organism and recommended initial intensive-phase intravenous antibiotic?
optionA: Klebsiella pneumoniae; intravenous ceftriaxone
optionB: Burkholderia pseudomallei (Melioidosis); intravenous meropenem or ceftazidime
optionC: Acinetobacter baumannii; intravenous ciprofloxacin
optionD: Pseudomonas aeruginosa; intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam
explanation: This presentation (wet season in northern Australia, diabetes/excess alcohol risk factors, pneumonia with visceral splenic/prostatic abscesses, oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod with bipolar staining and intrinsic resistance to aminoglycosides and polymyxins) is classic for melioidosis caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. Treatment requires at least 2–4 weeks of intensive intravenous therapy with meropenem (preferred in severe sepsis/ICU or neurological involvement) or ceftazidime, followed by a minimum of 3 months of eradication therapy with high-dose oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

questionText: A 59-year-old woman receiving R-CHOP chemotherapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma presents 10 days after her cycle with a temperature of 38.6°C. Her blood pressure is 116/72 mmHg, heart rate is 96 bpm, and she has no localising symptoms or signs of central venous catheter infection. Full blood count shows an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 0.2 x 10⁹/L. She has no penicillin allergy and no history of MRSA or ESBL colonisation. According to Australian Therapeutic Guidelines, what is the most appropriate immediate empirical intravenous antibiotic regimen?
optionA: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily
optionB: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6–8 hours (or cefepime 2 g every 8 hours)
optionC: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate plus ciprofloxacin
optionD: Intravenous vancomycin monotherapy
explanation: Febrile neutropenia (temperature >= 38.3°C or >= 38.0°C sustained over 1 hour with ANC < 0.5 x 10⁹/L) is a medical emergency requiring anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam administration within 60 minutes of presentation. In haemodynamically stable patients without penicillin allergy or MRSA risk factors, empirical monotherapy with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime is first-line. Ceftriaxone lacks Pseudomonas aeruginosa activity and is inadequate.

questionText: A 74-year-old hospitalised man develops profuse watery diarrhoea (6 stools/day) 8 days after completing a course of intravenous ceftriaxone for community-acquired pneumonia. His white cell count is 12.4 x 10⁹/L, serum creatinine is normal (78 umol/L), and stool PCR/toxin assay is positive for toxigenic Clostridioides difficile. This is his first episode. According to current international and Australian guidelines, which oral agent is most effective at achieving clinical cure and minimising recurrence?
optionA: Intravenous metronidazole 500 mg TDS
optionB: Oral vancomycin 125 mg QID or oral fidaxomicin 200 mg BD for 10 days
optionC: Intravenous vancomycin 1 g BD
optionD: Oral loperamide 4 mg stat then 2 mg after each loose stool
explanation: Oral vancomycin (125 mg four times daily for 10 days) or oral fidaxomicin (200 mg twice daily for 10 days) are superior to metronidazole for achieving sustained clinical resolution and reducing recurrence in Clostridioides difficile infection. Note that intravenous vancomycin is not excreted into the colonic lumen and is ineffective for C. difficile colitis.

questionText: A 68-year-old man undergoes colonoscopy after a positive faecal occult blood test and is found to have an ulcerated caecal adenocarcinoma. Prior to diagnosis, he had been admitted with prosthetic mitral valve infective endocarditis. Which blood culture isolate most strongly prompts colonoscopy to exclude an underlying colorectal neoplasia?
optionA: Streptococcus gallolyticus subsp. gallolyticus (formerly Streptococcus bovis biotype I)
optionB: Staphylococcus epidermidis
optionC: Haemophilus parainfluenzae
optionD: Enterococcus faecium
explanation: Bacteraemia or infective endocarditis caused by Streptococcus gallolyticus subsp. gallolyticus (formerly Streptococcus bovis biotype I) has a well-established association (25–80% of cases) with underlying colonic adenomas or colorectal carcinoma. All patients with S. gallolyticus bacteraemia or endocarditis must undergo full colonoscopy to exclude occult colonic malignancy.

questionText: Stem 1 of 3: A 36-year-old man survives an out-of-hospital ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest while sleeping. Restoring sinus rhythm reveals a spontaneous Type 1 coved ST-segment elevation of 3.5 mm in leads V1–V2. Coronary angiography and cardiac MRI are structurally normal. Select the most appropriate long-term intervention from the 10 options below.
optionA: Intravenous atropine 600 mcg bolus
optionB: Oral dapagliflozin 10 mg daily
optionC: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) insertion
optionD: Urgent surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement (AVR / TAVI)
optionsJson: {"A":"Intravenous atropine 600 mcg bolus","B":"Oral dapagliflozin 10 mg daily","C":"Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) insertion","D":"Urgent surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement (AVR / TAVI)","E":"Oral labetalol 100 mg BD","F":"Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg infusion","G":"Oral apixaban 5 mg BD","H":"Immediate electrical cardioversion","I":"Oral ivabradine 5 mg BD","J":"Urgent pericardiocentesis"}
explanation: In Brugada syndrome survivors of aborted sudden cardiac arrest or patients with spontaneous Type 1 ECG and arrhythmic syncope, secondary prevention with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD, Option C) is a Class I indication.

questionText: Stem 2 of 3: A 66-year-old woman with NYHA Class II heart failure (LVEF 32%) is in sinus rhythm at 78 bpm on maximum tolerated sacubitril/valsartan, carvedilol 25 mg BD, and spironolactone 25 mg daily. Her HbA1c is 5.3% and eGFR is 58 mL/min/1.73m². Select the agent from Options A–J that provides a Class I mortality and heart failure hospitalisation benefit.
optionA: Intravenous atropine 600 mcg bolus
